 ## Search results
Search results support adaptive history filtering, but did not establish a specific 2024–2026 time-aware gated NextItNet variant. Original [NextItNet](https://fajieyuan.github.io/papers/nextitnet6.pdf) uses residual causal dilated convolutions to expand receptive fields. [DyS4Rec (2025)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neunet.2025.107134) explicitly targets irrelevant historical interactions that obscure next-interaction intent. [Disentangle interest trend and diversity (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ipm.2023.103619) uses adaptive masking to distinguish dominant trends from scattered interests. These support selective history use, without proving that recent behavior should always dominate.

Practical hypothesis: retain one NextItNet backbone and add jointly trained sigmoid gates on dilated residual updates, conditioned on current hidden features and a causal recent-window summary. Gate shallow versus deeper representations before the shared item-scoring head, allowing the network to adjust its effective receptive field. This is an inferred architectural proposal, not a reported NextItNet result. Compare ungated, residual-gated, and recent-summary-gated variants using the fixed macro validation HR@10; read the final nonpadding position for left-padded histories.

If timestamps are available consistently during training and inference, add bucketed or log-scaled elapsed gaps to gate inputs. [Time-aware Attention Memory](https://durham-repository.worktribe.com/OutputFile/1140301) models temporal gates from elapsed intervals and interaction representations, providing precedent for content-dependent temporal weighting. Use only observed history timestamps, such as age relative to the latest observed interaction; never assume a future target timestamp. Without timestamps, position-based recent windows remain a valid ablation. All components should train jointly within one category model and checkpoint.

---

Recent work supports combining item text with behavioral supervision, but the retrieved 2024–2026 papers provide no verified direct match for a text encoder trained from scratch inside NextItNet. [ITS-Rec (2025)](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/9/1748) integrates titles, descriptions and reviews using BERT representations; its pretrained encoder and review inputs conflict with this task. [LLM2Emb (2026)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0957417426022840) highlights the central problem: textual similarity does not necessarily imply collaborative similarity. It tunes text representations using collaborative item pairs, but relies on pretrained LLMs and staged training.

Evidence for explicitly distinguishing substitutes from complements requires caution. [Knowledge-Guided Semantically Consistent Contrastive Learning (2025)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S089360802500070X) uses Amazon substitution/complementarity relationships to construct an item knowledge graph; those relationships are unavailable here. Purchase order alone does not establish either relation. [WhitenRec (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.10602) also reports insufficient discrimination among pretrained text embeddings, reinforcing the need to preserve item-specific information; its pretrained features and ensemble variant are unsuitable for this experiment.

A constraint-compatible hypothesis, rather than a demonstrated result from these papers: jointly learn separate title/description token pooling or small CNN encoders from random initialization, project their outputs into item-ID embeddings through a learned residual gate, and optimize the entire causal NextItNet with next-item supervision. Preserve model numbers, units and purpose-bearing phrases during tokenization. Keep ID embeddings to distinguish similarly described products, and let ordered interactions shape predictive relationships without assigning unobserved complement/substitute labels. This remains one jointly trained network and one checkpoint per category; validation must establish whether text improves HR@10.

---

Recent work supports gradually introducing informative negatives rather than immediately selecting the highest-scoring items. [R²NS (WWW 2026)](https://renzhaochun.github.io/assets/pdf/WWW_2026_Camera_Ready.pdf) combines uniform-sampling warm-up, efficient catalog-wide candidate recall, and curriculum reranking; it addresses early training instability and false negatives. [Scalable Cross-Entropy (RecSys 2024)](https://dspace.mit.edu/entities/publication/5392aca9-0bae-4176-9b3a-a8165957ba26) instead approximates full cross-entropy using maximum-inner-product selection of informative outputs. These provide sampling/objective ideas compatible in principle with retaining NextItNet’s causal dilated-convolution backbone; they do not establish gains on this benchmark.

[Correcting the LogQ Correction (RecSys 2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.09331) identifies a subtle sampled-softmax error: the positive is always included, whereas negatives are sampled. Its revised derivation treats those contributions separately and introduces an uncertainty-dependent weight, reporting improvements over standard logQ correction. Sampling correction addresses proposal-distribution bias; it does not identify genuinely relevant unobserved items. Earlier [UFNRec](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.04116) explicitly handles suspected false negatives through positive reassignment and teacher-provided soft labels, illustrating the distinction.

For Electronics, a reasonable experimental hypothesis is one NextItNet model trained with multiple negatives, uniform warm-up, then moderate-hardness sampling while excluding known training positives. Compare uncorrected sampled cross-entropy against a correction matched to the actual sampling distribution; deterministic top-k mining cannot simply inherit a popularity-based logQ formula.
